AI Summary

The two can't-miss papers this period are the major Cell review by Ho, Douse, and Marazzi — a sweeping synthesis of how TE DNA and RNA function as alternative promoters, exons, enhancers, 3D genome organizers, and lncRNA platforms across mammalian biology — and the Cell Reports study by Tanu et al. (Burns and Insco labs) showing that ZC3H18, a nuclear RNA surveillance factor lost in ~30% of human cancers, normally suppresses oncogenic ERV RNA, and that recurrent truncating mutations act dominantly to stabilize and relocalize ERV RNA to the cytoplasm, driving melanoma onset in zebrafish and sustaining human melanoma cell growth. The ZC3H18 finding is a direct mechanistic parallel to the lab's LTR10 enhancer work in CRC and SP140/ERV expression in ovarian cancer — raising the immediate question of whether ZC3H18 loss contributes to ERV RNA accumulation in PEO1 or HCT116 models. Also highly recommended: Schnabl-Baumgartner et al. in Molecular Cell, who show that the ChAHP complex (CHD4, ADNP, HP1) silences SINE B2 retrotransposons not via heterochromatin formation but by physically blocking TFIIIB recruitment to prevent Pol III transcription — a mechanistically distinct repression pathway that may be what keeps B2 SINEs silent until IFN signaling overrides it, as the lab demonstrated in mouse.

The digest is dominated by cGAS-STING, with six papers revealing distinct regulatory layers. At the structural level, Zhu et al. (top-ranked, score 120) map TREX1's specificity for dsDNA degradation to a single residue, R128, that contacts the non-substrate strand; autoimmune-associated TREX1 mutations at this interface increase cGAS-STING signaling and boost antitumor immunity in mice. Since TREX1 normally clears cytosolic DNA from TEs and other endogenous sources, this structural work directly informs how TE-derived DNA shifts the cGAS-STING activation threshold. New metabolic and nuclear functions add to the picture: Dong et al. (Immunity) show tumor-derived lactate, produced via PKM2-LDHA, directly binds and inhibits STING — a mechanism that PKM2 inhibition reverses, synergizing with anti-PD-1; Zhang Qimin et al. (Molecular Cell) reveal that PKCα phosphorylates cGAS at Ser120 to drive nuclear translocation where cGAS stabilizes β-catenin via TRIM33 displacement, activating Wnt signaling and TNBC metastasis entirely independently of STING; and Yasuda et al. show DRP1-deficient hyperfused mitochondria release mtRNA via BAX-dependent permeabilization, activating RIG-I-MAVS to enhance NK cell-mediated tumor killing — a cytosolic RNA-sensing mechanism parallel to TE RNA detection.

Several papers illuminate the regulatory evolution territory central to the lab. Zhu Kangli et al. (MBE) use deep learning across five primate genomes to show that ~50% of human CTCF binding sites are conserved and purifying-selected at TAD boundaries, while human-specific CBSs carry positive selection signatures and arise partly from TE sequences — exactly the kind of primate-specific regulatory innovation the lab documents with MER41 and Alu elements. Weaver and Lowe (MBE) show segmental duplications create >1,000 families of co-regulatory elements in human ESCs, with human-specific rewiring disproportionately expanding immune cell and neural gene regulatory networks — a parallel mechanism to TE-mediated co-regulatory network formation. On the SINE B2 front, the ChAHP paper above and the Kung et al. Genome Biology finding that pre-pachytene piRNAs map extensively to enhancers in human fetal testes — in a conserved amniote pattern — adds a new dimension: piRNAs originally studied for TE repression appear to regulate eRNA turnover as a somatic gene suppression mechanism in the germline.

Two RNA biology papers connect directly to the lab's splicing and isoform work. Guo et al. (Cell) achieve long-term reversal of Duchenne muscular dystrophy using circular ADAR-recruiting RNAs (circ-arRNAs) that drive exon skipping around DMD mutations — restoring dystrophin for >1.5 years in NHPs with a single AAV dose and showing safety and efficacy in a first-in-human study. The strategy of using RNA tools to redirect splicing at disease-causing exons is conceptually aligned with the lab's ASO splice-switching approach for the IFNAR2 Alu-derived exon. The NUMB isoform switch study (Genome Biology) adds to the pattern of oncogenic splicing switches: NUMB shifts from tumor-suppressive p66/p65 to oncogenic p72/p71 in tumors, altering Notch, WNT, Hedgehog, and Hippo signaling — the same isoform-function inversion logic that underlies the IFNAR2 decoy receptor system where Alu exonization produces a dominant-negative isoform.

▶ Genome Research RSS 40
The standout Genome Research paper this period is Samano et al.'s long-read pangenome study of 50 classical Drosophila phenotypes, finding structural variants — including TE insertions — underlie 67.4% of causal loci, validating that pangenome approaches reveal phenotypically important variation missed by short reads. A second paper by Zang et al. on TENNIS, a graph-based isoform inference algorithm, may also be of interest for TE-derived isoform discovery.

▶ Genome Biology RSS 51
A productive Genome Biology period with three top-ranked papers: Wehrkamp et al. on rapid TE-driven centromere evolution across the Avena genus; Kung et al. finding that pre-pachytene piRNAs map to enhancers in human fetal testes in a conserved amniote pattern; and the NUMB isoform switch study showing oncogenic p72/p71 isoforms alter multiple signaling pathways and predict poor breast cancer survival.

▶ Molecular Biology and Evolution PM 20
MBE delivered two directly relevant papers this period. Zhu Kangli et al. mapped CTCF binding site evolution across five primate species using deep learning, finding human-specific sites show positive selection and partly derive from TEs. Weaver and Lowe showed segmental duplications create >1,000 human co-regulatory element families with human-specific rewiring enriched in immune cells — a parallel mechanism to TE-mediated regulatory network formation.
